faculty_summary: Dr. Damir Cavar is an Associate Professor at Indiana University Bloomington, where he directs the Natural Language Processing Lab and organizes the Quantum AI and NLP Study Group. His research focuses on hybrid classical and quantum approaches to artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and reasoning systems, including the development of novel models and tools such as CBIRD and the Natural Language Qu Kit (NLQK). He is a core faculty member in multiple interdisciplinary centers at IU, spanning AI, data science, cybersecurity, quantum science, and cognitive science. A Senior Member of IEEE and a Senior Lifetime Member of ACM, Dr. Cavar actively contributes to the global AI and NLP community through research, innovation initiatives, and international collaborations.

The diversity of nematode mouthparts bears testament to this remarkable ability to specialize. faculty_summary: Broadly, I am motivated by understanding how variable and conflicting selective demands shape the evolution of organisms. The traits that interest me most are traits that are involved in trade-offs. For example, why would an organism attack a competitor, even if it meant certain death? How harmful should a parasite be to its hosts? When should a mother produce fewer offspring? My approach is to test theoretical predictions, either by manipulating the environment experimentally or comparing populations that differ in the field.

faculty_summary: Our lab’s broad interests are in plant-environment interactions, with the goals of understanding the mechanisms shaping plant and microbial community composition and diversity, ecosystem functioning, and system responses to abiotic and biotic environmental changes. Within these broad areas, we are especially interested in the importance of plant-soil and plant-microbe relationships and the role of environmental heterogeneity. faculty_summary: Sensory systems demonstrate an amazing ability to filter environmental information depending on the prevailing context. This ability allows animals to act appropriately in situations such as interaction with members of their species, or in response to potential threats. Sensory filtering is also important in human perception, as in hearing and understanding speech during social interactions, and in disorders in such perceptual processes. Work in my lab explores a neurochemical signal, serotonin, which is one of the mechanisms allowing the auditory system to filter important information.

faculty_summary: All organisms must perceive, process and react to environmental signals in order to survive and pass their genetic material onto the next generation. One of the most important signaling pathways for plant systems is that which begins with the perception of sunlight. This process, known as de-etiolation or “greening,” is mediated by the phytochrome (phy) family of photoreceptors. Upon absorption of red light, these photoreceptors translocate from the cytosol to the nucleus, where they bind to and trigger the degradation of a set of transcription factors known as PHYTOCHROME-INTERACTING FACTORS

faculty_summary: Dr. Sandra Kübler is a computational linguist whose research centers on machine learning approaches to natural language processing, with a strong emphasis on parsing morphologically rich languages such as German. Her work spans dependency parsing, part-of-speech tagging, corpus linguistics, and machine learning under class imbalance, as well as the detection of abusive and unsubstantiated information online. She has led and contributed to major interdisciplinary projects, including NSF-funded research on the spread of unsubstantiated information, and has worked on applications ranging from YouTube comment analysis to speech recognition and learner language assessment.
